deep.reconstruction:
The page has no text. It is a sheet of drawings on the back of a recycled IBM JES2 job-log listing dated 19 Aug 1982, which is printed upside down and is irrelevant to the mathematics. In the context of cote 154, 'systèmes de pseudo-droites', the drawings are best read as Grothendieck visualising arrangements of pseudo-lines in the real projective plane. He uses the standard model: a closed disk whose antipodal boundary points are identified. Any reading beyond what is visible is conjectural.

1. **Pseudo-line arrangements in a disk.** Several disks (centre, right, upper right) carry orange curves. Each runs from one boundary point to the roughly opposite one, and the curves cross each other pairwise. This is the usual picture of an arrangement of pseudo-lines in P^2(R).
2. **A grey pencil sketch (top right).** It shows a similar arrangement with marked dots on the boundary circle, apparently the 'points at infinity' where curves meet the boundary.
3. **Small blue semicircles on the boundary.** In two disks, small blue semicircles sit at the points where pseudo-lines reach the boundary circle. Plausibly they mark small neighbourhoods of the points at infinity: local pictures of how a pseudo-line crosses the line at infinity after antipodal gluing, or a local modification (cutting or blowing up) at those points. In one disk the green boundary is deformed by bumps, suggesting the boundary is being modified locally there.
4. **A disk with a dashed outer boundary tangent to an empty yellow circle.** Orange curves cross the tangency point, marked with small crosses. A plausible reading is two copies of the disk (two hemispheres) glued, i.e. the sphere S^2 as the double cover of P^2. Alternatively, it is a gluing operation joining two arrangements along a point or curve.
5. **A vertical chain of three tangent spheres.** One orange/red pseudo-line passes through all of them via the tangency points. This again suggests chaining or gluing local models, or a covering picture.
6. **A polygonal cell (lower left) with orange arrows radiating from a central point.** Blue segments run from the centre to the vertices and edges. This looks like the star of a vertex in the cell decomposition of P^2 induced by the arrangement. It may also be a dual picture: a cell with its barycentre, or the directions of lines through a point. That is consistent with Grothendieck's combinatorial, cellular ('carte') viewpoint seen on the next page, which shows coloured planar maps.

The previous page has labelled lists of points (p, q, r, ... with primes) and permutation-like symbols σ_0, σ_1, σ_2. This suggests the surrounding work encodes arrangements combinatorially, by the order of intersection points or by local sequences. The page states no theorem, construction or claim that can be read off with certainty.
